facts.fact_text: Hyde Park continued staging protests and demonstrations after removal from the Government's list of non-governmental organisations.

On 30 June 2006, Hyde Park (the first applicant) applied to the Chişinău Municipal Council for authorisation to hold a peaceful demonstration at the junction of Banulescu-Bodoni and Stefan cel Mare streets, not far from the Government building.
Hyde Park (the first applicant) requested authorisation to hold the demonstration between 1 and 31 August 2006.
The purpose of the demonstration was to protest against the refusal of the Moldovan Ministry of Culture to install a monument dedicated to the poet Liviu Rebreanu.
The monument dedicated to the poet Liviu Rebreanu had been donated by the Government of Romania.
On 30 August 2006 at 5 p.m., the applicants started their demonstration at the place indicated in the judgment of the Chişinău Court of Appeal of 29 August 2006.
On 30 August 2006 at 5.15 p.m., the applicants were approached by a group of police officers who asked whether they had authorisation for the demonstration.
The applicants showed the police officers the judgment of the Chişinău Court of Appeal of 29 August 2006 as authorisation for the demonstration.
In the police video, a police officer can be seen attempting to convince Mr Oleg Brega to stop the demonstration.
In the police video, Mr Oleg Brega refuses to stop the demonstration and argues that Hyde Park has a court judgment authorising the demonstration.
A person wearing a Special Forces uniform attacked one of the Hyde Park members from behind and violently threw him to the ground.
After the attack by the person in Special Forces uniform, the other demonstration participants were immediately surrounded by a group of police officers and taken to a police van.
Nobody among the demonstration participants appeared to resist arrest.
At the police station, police officers took the applicants' belongings including their mobile telephones.
The applicants were locked in different cells in groups of three or four persons at the police station.
The applicants were held in detention for approximately forty hours.
During the approximately forty hours of detention, the applicants were not provided with any food.
During detention, the applicants were only provided with water and occasionally taken to a toilet.
Only after the intervention of several human rights non-governmental organisations and after sixteen hours of detention were the applicants' relatives allowed to bring them food.
At court on 1 September 2006, the applicants learned about the charges against them for the first time.
The applicants were charged with holding an unauthorised demonstration contrary to Article 174 § 1 of the Moldovan Code of Administrative Offences.
The applicants were charged with resisting arrest contrary to Article 174 § 5 of the Moldovan Code of Administrative Offences.
The applicants were charged with insulting police officers contrary to Article 174 § 6 of the Moldovan Code of Administrative Offences.
On 18 July 2006, the Chişinău Municipal Council authorised the holding of a demonstration in writing, but only on 1 August 2006.
The Chişinău Municipal Council stated that it considered that one day of protest was sufficient in order to bring Hyde Park's concerns to the Government's attention.
On 25 July 2006, Hyde Park challenged the Chişinău Municipal Council's decision of 18 July 2006 in court.
On 29 August 2006, the Chişinău Court of Appeal found that the Chişinău Municipality's refusal to authorise the demonstration for the full requested period had been unlawful.
On 29 August 2006, the Chişinău Court of Appeal quashed the Chişinău Municipal Council's decision of 18 July 2006.

On 29 August 2006, the Chişinău Court of Appeal ordered the Chişinău Municipal Council to authorise Hyde Park (the first applicant) to hold a demonstration in front of the Government building between 29 and 31 August 2006.
The Chişinău Court of Appeal ordered that its judgment of 29 August 2006 should come into force immediately.
On 30 August 2006, the applicants requested authorisation from the Chişinău Municipality on the basis of the judgment of the Chişinău Court of Appeal of 29 August 2006.
The Chişinău Municipality refused to comply with the judgment of 29 August 2006 on the ground that it was not final.

Section 11(1) of the Moldovan Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that not later than fifteen days prior to the date of the assembly, the organiser shall submit a notification to the Municipal Council.

Section 11(2) of the Moldovan Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the prior notification shall indicate: the name of the organiser and the aim of the assembly; the date, starting time and finishing time; the location and access and return routes; the manner in which the assembly is to take place; the approximate number of participants; the persons who are to ensure and answer for the sound conduct of the assembly; and the services the organiser asks the Municipal Council to provide.

Section 11(3) of the Moldovan Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that if the situation so requires, the Municipal Council may alter certain aspects of the prior notification with the agreement of the organiser of the assembly.

Section 12(1) of the Moldovan Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the prior notification shall be examined by the local government of the town or village at the latest 5 days before the date of the assembly.

Section 12(2) of the Moldovan Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that when the prior notification is considered at an ordinary or extraordinary meeting of the Municipal Council, the discussion shall deal with the form, timetable, location and other conditions for the conduct of the assembly and the decision taken shall take account of the specific situation.

Section 12(6) of the Moldovan Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the local authorities can reject an application to hold an assembly only if after having consulted the police, it has obtained convincing evidence that the provisions of sections 6 and 7 will be breached with serious consequences for society.

Section 14(1) of the Moldovan Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that a decision rejecting the application for holding an assembly shall be reasoned and presented in writing and shall contain reasons for refusing to issue the authorisation.
Section 15(1) of the Moldovan Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the organiser of the assembly can challenge the refusal in the administrative courts.

Section 6(1) of the Moldovan Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies shall be conducted peacefully, without any sort of weapons, and shall ensure the protection of participants and the environment, without impeding the normal use of public highways, road traffic and the operation of economic undertakings and without degenerating into acts of violence capable of endangering the public order and the physical integrity and life of persons or their property.

Section 7 of the Moldovan Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies shall be suspended in circumstances including: denial and defamation of the State and of the people; incitement to war or aggression and incitement to hatred on ethnic, racial or religious grounds; incitement to discrimination, territorial separatism or public violence; and acts that undermine the constitutional order.

Section 8(1) of the Moldovan Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies may be conducted in squares, streets, parks and other public places in cities, towns and villages, and also in public buildings.

Section 8(2) of the Moldovan Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that it shall be forbidden to conduct an assembly in the buildings of the public authorities, the local authorities, prosecutors' offices, the courts or companies with armed security.

Section 8(3)(a) of the Moldovan Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that it shall be forbidden to conduct assemblies within fifty metres of the parliament building, the residence of the President of Moldova, the seat of the government, the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court of Justice.

Section 8(3)(b) of the Moldovan Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that it shall be forbidden to conduct assemblies within twenty-five metres of the buildings of the central administrative authority, the local public authorities, courts, prosecutors' offices, police stations, prisons and social rehabilitation institutions, military installations, railway stations, airports, hospitals, companies which use dangerous equipment and machines, and diplomatic institutions.
A person wearing a Special Forces uniform attacked one of the Hyde Park members from behind and violently threw him to the ground.
After the attack by the person in Special Forces uniform, the other demonstration participants were immediately surrounded by a group of police officers and taken to a police van.
Nobody among the demonstration participants appeared to resist arrest.
The applicants were locked in different cells in groups of three or four persons at the police station.
The two female applicants were put in a separate cell at the police station.
According to the applicants, they were not allowed to make any telephone calls while detained at the police station.
According to the applicants, they were not allowed to consult a lawyer while detained at the police station.
According to the applicants, the cells at the police station were small, humid and dirty.
According to the applicants, the cells at the police station smelled of urine and faeces.
According to the applicants, the cells at the police station did not have windows.
According to the applicants, the electric light in the cells at the police station was always on.
According to the applicants, there were only two wooden benches inside each cell at the police station.
The applicants were held in detention for approximately forty hours.
During the approximately forty hours of detention, the applicants were not provided with any food.
During detention, the applicants were only provided with water and occasionally taken to a toilet.
Only after the intervention of several human rights non-governmental organisations and after sixteen hours of detention were the applicants' relatives allowed to bring them food.

The Buiucani District Court found that after obtaining the favourable judgment from the Chişinău Court of Appeal of 29 August 2006, the applicants should have applied to the Chişinău Municipal Council for authorisation.
The Buiucani District Court fined each applicant except Mr Oleg Brega 200 Moldovan lei (MDL).
The Buiucani District Court fined Mr Oleg Brega, who was the president of Hyde Park at the time, MDL 500.
On 1 November 2006, the Supreme Court of Justice quashed the judgment of the Chişinău Court of Appeal of 29 August 2006.
On 1 November 2006, the Supreme Court of Justice dismissed the applicants' action, finding that the Chişinău Municipal Council's decision of 18 July 2006 was lawful.
The Supreme Court of Justice ruled that the ruling of the Chişinău Court of Appeal concerning the immediate enforcement of its judgment of 29 August 2006 had been unlawful.
On 18 September 2006, the applicants lodged a criminal complaint against the police officers who had arrested them.
In their criminal complaint of 18 September 2006, the applicants complained that they had been abused by the police officers who arrested them.
In their criminal complaint of 18 September 2006, the applicants complained that they had been illegally detained.
In their criminal complaint of 18 September 2006, the applicants complained that their right to privacy of correspondence had been violated.
In their criminal complaint of 18 September 2006, the applicants complained that their right to freedom of assembly had been violated.
In their criminal complaint of 18 September 2006, the applicants complained that they had suffered inhuman and degrading treatment.
In their criminal complaint of 18 September 2006, the applicants complained of the refusal to execute court decisions.
Between September 2006 and September 2007, the criminal proceedings initiated at the applicants' request were dismissed and re-opened four times.
On each occasion between September 2006 and September 2007, the Prosecutor's Office dismissed the applicants' criminal complaint.
On each occasion between September 2006 and September 2007, the courts or the hierarchically superior prosecutor quashed the Prosecutor's Office's decision to dismiss and ordered a re-examination.

The reasons for the Prosecutor's Office's dismissals included the testimonies of police officers and police witnesses who confirmed the allegations that the applicants had insulted the police and resisted arrest.

Regarding the allegation concerning tampering with the applicants' mobile telephones and deleting files from them, the Prosecutor's Office accepted the testimony of a police officer who confirmed that two mobile telephones had been seized during the applicants' detention but denied the allegations that somebody had tampered with them.
Regarding the video of the event filmed by the police representatives, the Prosecutor's Office argued that it had been lost and that, therefore, it could not be examined.
On 27 September 2007, the Rascani District Court quashed the last decision dismissing the applicants' complaints and ordered a re-examination.
After 27 September 2007, the applicants did not hear any more from the Prosecutor's Office about the status of their complaint.
On 10 January 2008, the applicants wrote to the Prosecutor General's Office to enquire as to the stage reached in their proceedings.
The applicants did not receive a reply from the Prosecutor General's Office to their letter of 10 January 2008.
A copy of the applicants' letter of 10 January 2008 with a stamp of the Prosecutor General's Office on it was annexed to the applicants' observations.
According to the applicants, it was only from the Government's observations that they learned that their complaint had been dismissed again on 12 November 2007.
The Government disputed the applicants' submissions concerning the letter of 10 January 2008 which the applicants stated they had sent to the Prosecutor General's Office.
The Government did not dispute the authenticity of the Prosecutor General's stamp on the copy of the applicants' letter of 10 January 2008.
